questions.q: Reorder: 'yesterday / the match / won / our team'.
questions.a: 'Our team won the match yesterday.' A wrong answer 'Yesterday won our team the match' shows the student treats 'yesterday' as a movable prefix without checking what still makes grammatical sense.

questions.q: Do these mean the same? 'Only Ravi ate the mango' / 'Ravi ate only the mango.'
questions.a: No — 'only' attaches to what follows it: first says nobody else ate, second says he ate nothing else. A wrong answer 'yes' reveals the student thinks 'only' floats freely — position changes meaning.

questions.q: Fix: 'To school every day goes Meena.'
questions.a: 'Meena goes to school every day.' A wrong answer keeping verb-first order shows the student is translating Hindi SOV word order — English needs the verb between subject and object.

questions.q: Word order is not ______ — English meaning rides on position.
Fill in the blank: Word order is not ______ — English meaning rides on position. 'The dog chased the cat' and 'The cat chased the dog' use the same words to say opposite things.
Fill in the blank: Then the trap pair: 'Ravi helped Mohan' vs 'Mohan helped Ravi' — same words, ______ helpers.
What is Word order? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Word order is not decoration — English meaning rides on position. 'The dog chased the cat' and 'The cat chased the dog' use the same words to say opposite things.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Word order?
questions.a: Students accept any order that 'sounds okay' from spoken English — especially putting time phrases anywhere — and don't notice when actor and receiver swap silently.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student rearranges jumbled words into a grammatical S–V–O sentence, preserves meaning while reordering phrases, and detects when a rearrangement silently flips actor and receiver.
